extracted.intended_audience: public relations managers, PR students, and organizational decision-makers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for budgeting, scheduling, selecting, and evaluating public relations programs using PERT/CPM, cost-benefit and expected-value analyses, simplified programming, and program-specific evaluation metrics. Focuses on choosing alternatives for publics under resource constraints and measuring program effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical path (definition and management)
rubrics_metrics.description: The path through a project network that takes the longest time and therefore defines the shortest possible time in which a project can be completed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Managers must pay particular attention to the critical path because you cannot shorten overall project time without reducing time on one or more activities along the critical path; exceeding estimated time for any activity on the critical path will lengthen the project. If you shorten the critical path, verify another path does not become the new critical path.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slack (noncritical path excess time)
rubrics_metrics.description: Excess time available on noncritical paths that can be used without delaying project completion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use slack to reassign people or resources from noncritical to critical activities to speed the project, or delay the start of noncritical activities to free resources. Slack provides managerial flexibility for scheduling.

rubrics_metrics.name: CPM time estimates: normal time vs crash time
rubrics_metrics.description: In CPM managers estimate two times per activity: a 'normal time' using normal operating procedures and a 'crash time' representing the shortest time when resources are fully applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct network charts using crash times to find minimum possible project time; construct a second network with normal times to compare critical paths. Recognize crash time implies higher resource/cost expenditure.

rubrics_metrics.name: CPM crash-cost minimization procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: A procedure to determine the minimum cost to achieve the shortest project duration by selectively 'crashing' activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate crash cost of activities on the critical path, select the activity with the lowest crash cost and reduce its time to crash time, then re-evaluate the critical path. Repeat selecting the least-cost activity on the (possibly new) critical path until the project time equals the minimum crash network time; the sum spent is the minimum crash cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two fundamental decisions in selecting PR programs
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) Which is the best alternative to reach each public? (2) Which publics are most important and deserve priority given limited resources?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Answer (1) by using situational theory (match technique & medium to public). Answer (2) by prioritizing programs that maximize resource use and contribute most to organizational goals, using analytic techniques described (expected value, simplified programming).

rubrics_metrics.name: Technique and medium selection by public type (Grunig situational theory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Select techniques and media appropriate to the public's communication behavior: actively communicating publics vs passively communicating publics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively communicating publics: use written information, print media, and provide in-depth information (they seek information). Passively communicating publics: use visual media, simple and short messages, pictures and illustrations to gain attention and promote processing/retention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical choice rule under constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple alternative strategies exist to reach a public, usually choose the alternative that costs the least and can be implemented most easily within your time constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance cost, ease of implementation, and time; however, when resources limit implementation across multiple publics, use analytic methods (expected-value/simplified programming) to maximize return per dollar and day.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-benefit analysis principle (qualitative application)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the costs of a program with the monetary (or estimated) value of its benefits; implement programs only when benefits exceed costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because monetizing PR benefits (understanding, attitude change) is extremely difficult, use the cost-benefit concept qualitatively to choose programs that maximize benefits for resources spent rather than trying to compute exact dollar values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expected-value analysis (formulae for PR programs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate the expected value of a PR program by multiplying an estimated payoff value by the probability that the payoff will occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Expected Value = ProbInfoSeek × EstPayoffValue for strategies aiming at information seeking. Use Expected Value = 1/2 × ProbInfoProcess × EstPayoffValue for strategies aiming at information processing (information-processed messages are treated as about half as effective as information-sought). Probabilities may be taken from empirical tables (e.g., Table 7-2) or estimated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assigning payoff values based on linkage types
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate payoff values for communicating with publics based on their linkage to the organization: enabling, input/output functional, normative, or diffused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give high value to enabling-linkage publics (e.g., funding/regulatory agencies) because they can threaten survival; give high value to input/output publics (employees/customers) if they have refused to cooperate or market competition is strong; assign high value to normative-linkage publics if the organization can gain from their information/support; assign high value to diffused-linkage publics that could organize to pressure, embarrass, or restrict the organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparing expected values across publics (use for priority setting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiply payoff values by appropriate probabilities to compute expected values for programs aimed at different publics, then rank programs by expected value to guide resource allocation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remember to adjust for the difference between probabilities of information seeking vs processing (multiply processing by 1/2). Use computed expected values to prioritize programs, but also consider resource costs—high expected-value programs that exceed resource constraints may be infeasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linear programming applicability criteria (four requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: To use linear programming the manager must: (1) have a quantitative goal to maximize or minimize; (2) have alternative means to accomplish the goal; (3) face scarce resources; and (4) be able to express exchanges between alternatives mathematically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For PR, use expected value as the quantitative goal, alternatives are different PR programs, scarce resources are money and time, and you must be able to express resource usage per program. Note: classical linear programming assumes divisibility which often does not hold for PR programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplified programming (variation of linear programming for PR)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practical variation of linear programming that overcomes indivisibility of PR programs and can be done without a computer to allocate scarce resources to programs to maximize expected value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a stepwise tabular method: list total resources and each program’s money/time requirements and expected values; choose the highest expected-value program that fits resource constraints; allocate resources, subtract used resources, reconstruct the table with remaining programs and resources, and repeat until resources exhausted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indivisibility caveat for PR programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations programs usually are not divisible— you cannot produce 'fractional' programs—making direct application of classical linear programming difficult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use simplified programming to handle indivisibility: select whole programs sequentially by highest feasible expected value given remaining constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation is essential (prove PR value to management)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations must now demonstrate with hard evidence that programs meet objectives and contribute to organizational goals; evaluation research is essential to avoid budget cuts or elimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Managers should adopt measurement practices similar to other organizational functions and prepare to answer 'What's this worth to us?'. Ongoing measurement programs (e.g., AT&T) illustrate institutionalized evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation objective: communication behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure whether communication actually took place (a behavior: movement of symbols from organization to a public).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For press relations, measure whether the organization communicated with media (e.g., number of clippings originating from press reps). This is a basic, observable objective distinct from effects like attitude change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation objective: message retention and accuracy/understandability
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure how well target audiences remember messages and how understandable they found the messages (measures of accuracy and retention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use surveys to ask recipients whether they received publications, recall specific article content, and rate understandability; use readability measures for publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation objective: acceptance of cognitions and overt behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure whether audiences accept communicated cognitions (knowledge/beliefs) and exhibit intended behaviors as a result of PR programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track downstream indicators (acceptance metrics, behavioral outcomes) where feasible. Note the text recommends focusing evaluation primarily on communication and retention because effects on attitudes/behavior are harder to predict and measure reliably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press-relations evaluation metrics and procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate press relations by content-analyzing media coverage to determine origin, messages communicated, reflection of intended themes, and tone (favorable/neutral/unfavorable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use computerized tabulation to count clippings, identify which originated from company efforts, tally theme presence, and classify sentiment; track these measures over time (monthly/annual trends).

rubrics_metrics.name: Employee-communication evaluation metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess employee communication via annual surveys to measure receipt of publications, message recall, perceived understandability, and publication readability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine objective measures (distribution counts, readability scores) with surveys to assess retention and comprehension; these provide measures of whether objectives were met (communication and accuracy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Community-relations evaluation metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure both the frequency/use of community-relations techniques (open houses, interviews, talks) and the effects of these activities on message retention, acceptance of cognitions, and overt behaviors of community leaders/residents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin by documenting activities; follow with evaluation studies to assess changes in retention, attitudes, or behaviors resulting from the activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational-relations evaluation metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate educational programs by measuring the extent to which target learners (e.g., schoolchildren) learned the themes presented in materials provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tests, surveys, or observational measures in educational settings to assess theme learning attributable to provided materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program-specific evaluation requirement (avoid broad polling for program evaluation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation must be specific to individual programs; broad polls of public attitudes are useful for environmental scanning but not adequate for evaluating program effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design evaluation measures tailored to the program’s stated communication objectives (communication occurrence, retention, acceptance, behavior) rather than relying on general attitude polls.
